title: Job classes with one or two holders in the whole City
question: Which job classes are held by only one or two people citywide, what are they paid, and which have been held by the same single person all along?
finding: In fiscal 2026, 120 of the 955 job classes in use had exactly one paid holder in the whole City and 79 had two; together they were paid $46.7 million. In 38 of the one-holder classes the present holder is the only person the payroll has ever named in it; 16 have had the same single holder in every year since fiscal 2017, the first year with names. 50 of the one-holder posts are exempt from civil-service hiring and 7 of the one- and two-holder classes carry a generic title. One-holder classes numbered 170 in fiscal 2013.
how: City payroll file, fiscal years 2013 to 2026. A holder is anyone paid in the class during the year. Seats on boards and commissions, elected offices and the Superior Court’s own classes are left out. “Sole holder since” counts back from fiscal 2026 for as long as the same one name is the only holder; 2017 means the whole period for which the file has names. Generic titles are listed first, then the longest-held one-person classes, by pay. Titles are printed as the payroll prints them (Dep Dir is deputy director, Dept Head is department head, Sprv is supervisor).
limits: A class with one holder is usually a specialist or the head of something: the list itself includes a chief medical examiner, a head airport electrician and a chief plumbing inspector; others are the last person left in a class that is no longer filled. A long-serving sole holder is what one would expect in such a post. The list shows where a title and a person coincide; whether the class was written for the person can only be seen in the job-classification record (when the class was created and at whose request) and the job announcement. People are named because the payroll names them; nothing here says any of them did anything wrong.
